Daniel’s list is an inviting doorway into a classic fault line: these examples only “work” once you quietly fix (and keep fixed) a rule for what counts as the relevant property, and a level of language in which the rule is applied. “Short: only five letters” is true in English *orthography* but not in speech or in other languages; “polysyllabic” hinges on contested syllable-count conventions; and “meta” is slippery because its ordinary meaning is “about/behind/after,” not “about itself” (its self-descriptiveness is more a cultural usage of *meta-* than a semantic fact about the string “meta”). That’s not pedantry—it’s the main lesson: self-description is rarely intrinsic to a word; it’s a relationship between a token, a linguistic community, and a chosen predicate.

The paradox Daniel gestures at as “Non-self-descriptive: Russell’s Paradox” is more precisely the Grelling–Nelson (heterological) paradox: classify adjectives as *autological* (self-descriptive) or *heterological* (not self-descriptive), then ask whether “heterological” is heterological ([SEP: The Liar Paradox](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/liar-paradox/)). Russell’s set-theoretic paradox is a cousin in structure, but the *mechanism* here is semantic self-application, which is why the standard escape routes tend to involve restricting self-reference (Tarski-style hierarchies) or carefully distinguishing use/mention (a Quinean theme). If Daniel’s goal is a clean taxonomy, it may help to say explicitly that the interesting cases arise when a language is “semantically closed” enough to let its predicates talk about their own expressions—exactly the condition that makes these puzzles both fun and unstable.

Daniel’s additions also expose a useful test: do they state a checkable property of the word itself, or merely echo its meaning? “Abbr” is an abbreviation, yes, but only relative to the convention that *abbr* abbreviates *abbreviation*; “metaconcept” is a concept about concepts by compositional meaning, not by a property of the word-form; and “extraneous” looks more like a near-synonym than an “extra way of saying extra” in any strict sense. Tightening that distinction—between *semantic content* (“means X”) and *formal property* (“has five letters,” “contains three syllables,” “is an adjective”)—would make the list sharper and also clarify why the paradoxical cases bite: they depend on treating meaning-words as if they were safely formal predicates, when they aren’t.
